world.bio: Registered nurse on the night shift at a dementia care home in Chorlton. Twenty years in nursing, the last six here. I know which residents sundown around four in the afternoon, which ones want the landing light left on, and which ones will only take their tablets from a particular carer. Divorced two years, one teenage son, one border collie called Biscuit. At 42 I am learning to drive, and I have failed the test twice on roundabouts.
skills_assets: RGN registration, twenty years in nursing, six in dementia care
Night shifts four nights on, three off, so most afternoons are mine to sleep through
A rented terraced house in Stretford with a small back yard
A provisional licence and a patient driving instructor named Colm
A border collie who needs two long walks a day
A small circle of colleagues who swap shifts without fuss

projects.name: Pass the driving test
projects.text: Third attempt booked for 14 October. I failed twice on roundabouts; the examiner said I hesitated and then went at the wrong moment. Colm has me doing roundabouts in the Trafford Park industrial estate on Sunday mornings when it is empty. My goal is simple: stop depending on two buses and a thirty-minute walk at 7 a.m. after a night shift.

projects.name: Memory boxes for the residents
projects.text: I am putting together a memory box for each resident on my corridor: a shoebox with a few photographs, a bit of fabric, a small object they used to own. Families bring things in, and the residents love it. The unit manager says it takes too much time. I do it on quiet nights anyway, and I have finished seven of the twelve.

notes.text: Night shift. Mr. Alderton woke at 3 and asked me where his wife had gone. She died in 2019. I sat with him and said she had gone to the shops and would be back soon. It is not a lie that makes me feel good, but it lets him sleep. I always wonder who I am protecting.

Driving lesson, 4 p.m. Colm made me do the same roundabout seven times. By the seventh I could do it with my eyes shut, which is not recommended, he said. He is a very calm man. I think he practises calm on me.
Jack ate dinner standing at the open fridge. We exchanged exactly two sentences: "pass the milk" and "no". He is sixteen and has turned into a very polite lodger.

Mrs. Okonkwo hit a carer today. The carer, Fiona, did not flinch. At handover she said "it is the illness, not her". I wanted to hug her and instead said "tea?". Nursing is mostly saying "tea?" when you want to say something else.

Biscuit ate a whole packet of chocolate digestives off the counter. Vet said he will be fine. I spent two hours Googling "dog chocolate toxicity" and took him for an extra walk, which I felt was a fair punishment for both of us.

Slept with blackout curtains until 5 p.m. Woke up not knowing if it was morning or evening, ate cereal at the window, watched a boy on the street kick a ball against a wall for forty minutes. I felt like I was in a film about a woman who has no days.
Ex rang about the weekend. Jack wants to stay with him on the 3rd. I said that is fine and then sat on the stairs. Being fine takes effort.
Birthday of my dad who died. I made his shortbread. It came out too crumbly. He would have said "lovely, love" and eaten four.
Unit manager called a meeting about the staffing. Two nurses leaving. She asked if I would do an extra night a week. I said I would think. Thinking is what I do instead of saying no.
Colm said I am ready. I said that is what he said last time. He said last time I was not ready and he was lying. I laughed so hard I stalled the car.

messages.text: Fiona: Can you swap Thursday? Me: I can if you do my Saturday. Fiona: Done. Me: You owe me a doughnut. Fiona: Two.
Me: Dinner at 6? Jack: ok. Me: What do you want? Jack: whatever. Me: I made pasta. Jack: fine. Me: Love you. Jack: ok.
Colm: Sunday at 8 in the industrial estate. Bring a flask. Me: I will bring two. Colm: Do not bring Biscuit. Me: He is in the back seat already.
Tom: Can Jack stay Friday to Sunday? Me: Yes, check with him. Tom: He says he wants to. Me: Then it is fine. Tom: Thanks, Dee.
Mum: Are you eating? Me: Yes. Mum: Properly? Me: Cereal counts. Mum: It does not.

calendar.event: Practice on empty roundabouts, Trafford Park, 8 a.m.

relations.about: Sixteen, lives mostly in his room, speaks to me through the fridge door
Civil, mostly; he lives in Salford with his new partner
Patient, laughs at my jokes more than he should
Another night nurse, the person I trust most at work

constraints: Cannot work more than four nights in a row
Needs to be home by 8:30 a.m. to catch Jack before school
Tight budget: the test fee and lessons are already stretching the month
sensitive: Still grieves the marriage and does not talk about it
Terrified of failing the test a third time
Quietly worried about burnout; has not taken a proper holiday in three years
